info.name: ThunderID - Resource Sharing Demo
info.description: Demonstrates the B2B sharing of resource servers, resources, and actions across organization units: three separate sharing-framework resource types (resource_server/resource/action) so a specific action can be withheld while its sibling is shared; cascade share fanning a single call out to every descendant; cascade exclusion via excludedNodeIds; a newly created action auto-inheriting its parent's active share with no separate call; cascade unshare tearing down every descendant grant created alongside the one revoked; write-time defense in depth against naming a permission not currently visible to the caller's own organization unit; the deployment root permission's categorical bypass; and, the actual point of the whole feature, a compound RBAC check proving a role's stored permissions are not enough by themselves, only what is both assigned AND currently shared is honored by real client_credentials token issuance. See B2B-Reference/B2B_RESOURCE_SHARING_DESIGN.md for the full design and api/resource.yaml for the REST API reference these requests exercise. This collection is deliberately scoped to what is new/different about resource-server/resource/action sharing; the underlying OU-targeting mechanics (allRoots/allChildren/rootOuIds/ouIds, exclusion, one-hop delegation chains, cross-tree restrictions) are inherited unchanged from the generic sharing framework and are already fully proven by B2B-Reference/role-sharing. It also pins the Resource Management API's own authorization boundary: the system:resource-servers/system:resource-servers:view scope split and the per-caller organization unit confinement layered on top of it, whose three refusal layers (AUTH-4030, RES-1024, SHR-1007) folder '07' keeps deliberately distinguishable.

item.name: 07 - API Authorization: system:resource-servers Scope
Look Up the System Resource Server's 'system' Resource

request.description: Resolves the bootstrap-fixed System resource server's top-level 'system' resource id dynamically, rather than assuming the deterministic <systemResourceServerId>_system id shape. The two sub-resources created below are nested under it, which is what derives the system:resource-servers and system:resource-servers:view permission strings the API's own authorization gate matches on (backend/internal/system/security/permissions.go).

item.name: Create 'Resource Servers' Sub-Resource Under System Resource

request.description: Nesting a 'Resource Servers' resource under the 'system' resource via parent, rather than as a top-level resource, is what derives the permission string system:resource-servers (parent resource's own permission, the delimiter, then this resource's handle) instead of a flat 'resource-servers'. That string is the manage tier the Resource Management API requires on POST, PUT, and DELETE.

item.name: Create 'View' Sub-Resource Under Resource Servers Resource

request.description: Derives system:resource-servers:view, the read-only counterpart the API requires on GET /resource-servers and GET /resource-servers/**. The manage permission covers it by hierarchical prefix matching, so a system:resource-servers caller can read too, but not the reverse.

item.name: B (Manage): Attempt Create Resource Server in A (Rejected)

request.description: The scope check passes, and the request is still refused. Neither system:resource-servers nor its view counterpart carries a subtree tier, so requireOwnOUScope confines the caller to the organization unit its own token was issued for (RES-1024). Checked before any organization unit lookup, so the endpoint cannot be used to probe which organization unit ids exist.

item.name: B (Manage): Attempt Create Resource Under A's Resource Server (Rejected)

request.description: The same confinement applies one level down: A's resource server being shared to B lets B read it, never write into it.

item.name: B (Manage): Attempt Create Action Under A's Bookings Resource (Rejected)

request.description: Bookings is currently shared to B, and creating an action under it is still refused: the confinement is evaluated against the owning resource server's organization unit, not against share visibility.

item.name: B (Manage): Attempt Update A's Resource Server (Rejected)

request.description: Updating an existing record defers to sharing.RequireOwnership rather than requireOwnOUScope, so the error is the sharing framework's own SHR-1007 and not RES-1024. Same refusal, different owner of the rule: core configuration may only ever be changed by the owning organization unit.

item.name: B (Manage): Attempt Delete A's Resource Server (Rejected)

request.description: Also SHR-1007, via RequireOwnershipForDeletion. internal/resource declares no deletion specific ownership error of its own, unlike internal/role, so deletion and core-config edits report the same code. Refused before any deletion is attempted, so A's resource server survives for the Cleanup folder.

item.name: B (Manage): Get A's Bookings Resource via Share Fallback

request.description: The positive contrast for the two refusals below: Bookings belongs to A, but it is currently shared to B, so RequireVisibility's share fallback applies and the read succeeds.

item.name: B (Manage): Attempt Get A's Refunds Resource (Rejected, Not Shared)

request.description: Refunds sits under the same resource server as Bookings and was excluded from every cascade, so neither branch of RequireVisibility holds: not B's own organization unit, and not shared to it. Being able to read the parent resource server buys nothing here.

item.name: B (Manage): Attempt Get A's approve Action (Rejected, Not Shared)

request.description: The identical check at the action tier, the third of the three sharing-framework resource types.

item.name: No Resource-Servers Scope: Rejected at Global Gate

request.description: A token holding neither system, system:resource-servers, nor system:resource-servers:view never reaches internal/resource at all, so the response is the security middleware's own AUTH-4030 rather than any RES code.

B (Manage): Delete Own Resource Invoices

request.description: The last of the three manage-tier writes on a resource server the caller owns, and this folder's own teardown of it. A resource server cannot be deleted while resources or actions still depend on it, hence the order.

item.name: Unshare A's Resource Server Grant (Restore Folder 05's State)

request.description: Issued with the collection's root-scoped admin token. Tears down the re-share this folder created, along with every descendant grant that came with it, leaving A's resource server unshared again as folder '05' left it.

item.description: The Resource Management API's own token-scope tier, independent of the sharing model the folders above exercise. system:resource-servers grants full access (create, update, delete, share); system:resource-servers:view grants read-only access, exactly mirroring Role Management's split. On top of the scope check, a caller without the deployment root permission is confined to the organization unit its own token was issued for, so this folder separates three distinct refusals that all answer 403 and are easy to conflate: AUTH-4030 from the security middleware when the scope itself is insufficient, RES-1024 from internal/resource when the scope is right but the target organization unit is not the caller's own (and not shared to it), and SHR-1007 from the sharing framework when an existing record's owner is someone else. The two scoped tokens are minted for B, the sharee, not for A, the owner. Every request overrides the collection-level bearer auth with one of them, except the fixture setup and the final unshare, which use the root-scoped admin token.
